pilot.summary: Three-player pod at Tom's, me on Edgar, Alex on Sauron, Tom on blue-black. Five vampires down by turn three off three mana spent, and the whole table made Markov the problem immediately — I ate multiple wipes and a stack of counters, and rebuilt in a turn or two every time. I did not cast Edgar until I had eight mana, which is my own mistake; when he landed it was the finisher, and Olivia's Wrath into a wide haste swing got Alex to 1. Tom countered Champion of Dusk and Bloodthirsty Conqueror, I needed one more vampire, and had nothing.

Five-player pod at Oliver's, second game of the night, seat 5. Mulliganed once and kept a two-land hand out of stubbornness — I knew at the time it should have gone back. Blood Artist and Bloodthirsty Conqueror landed early and a wipe with the drain online killed eleven creatures: every opponent lost 11, I gained 11, and I was around 50 to the table's 20. Then Ryan's recurring artifact and enchantment removal picked off Anointed Procession and the rest, I ran out of steam with vampires on board and nothing in hand, and Deflecting Swat and Teferi's Protection sat uncast all game because the mana was always spent on vampires.

Three-player pod at Alex's in Orinda, game two of four, me against Alex and Stuart. "Best-case opener and it did not matter" — two lands plus Sol Ring into a Talisman, four mana on turn one, Edgar down fast, Warleader's Call and the token-enters enchantments in place — and then Edgar was the only vampire I cast all game. Got Alex to 12 commander damage before he assembled blockers and he closed later with an oversized threat; I ran out of steam on card draw again. The conversation with Alex afterwards is the part that matters: the deck changes direction from swarm typal to lords and payoffs, tokens become the dig engine, and the token-conversion axis from 25 August is withdrawn.

Five-player pod at Oliver's, game three of three, first night on the twelve-swap list. Tom's Goblin Sharpshooter pinged my tokens and that fed the card-draw creatures, so I was running my engine off his removal. I resolved a big flyer that draws cards, brought Edgar down, then pivoted to Bloodletter of Aclazotz for the doubled damage and swung lethal into Alex to take him out. Tom tutored a two-card infinite and closed before my lethal resolved — a loss with Edgar dominating the board, and one I want on record as unsatisfying in a way that losing to a better board is not.

read.what_it_does: On v1.1.0 it opens with an eminence token swarm and then gets paid when those bodies die. Tom's Goblin Sharpshooter pinged my tokens all game and that fed the pay-two-life draw creatures, so I was running my engine off his removal (004). Combat is still how it actually threatens to close: the lethal was Bloodletter of Aclazotz for doubled damage into a wide Edgar swing that took Alex out (004), which is worth holding against engine.json's thesis that the two proven kill routes need no combat damage. On V1 the same opening built a wide board that then ran dry (001, 002, 003).
read.how_it_plays: Fast and completely visible. Five vampires by turn three off three mana spent, and the whole table decided Edgar was the problem immediately (001) — that is the price of the plan, not a surprise. It absorbs an enormous amount: multiple wipes and a stack of counters in one game with a real board back in a turn or two every time (001), and it was still among the last players standing in a five-player pod (002). Where it ends up is board-dominant and beaten by something the board cannot answer — a tutored two-card infinite (004), a counter on the refuel (001), a wipe with nothing left in hand (002).
mindful_of: You are the archenemy from turn three and the table's answers come at you first (001). My own read at the time: that is the correct read, and the price of the plan.

Edgar's cast is a decision, not what happens when the mana is spare. He came down at eight in the game where the turn he landed was the turn that got Alex to 1, and the reason I gave was 'I had not even been thinking about him' (001).
The refuel is what gets countered. Champion of Dusk — the draw-five that would have closed it — and Bloodthirsty Conqueror both ate counters in one game (001), and both are still in the 99.

Protection stays in hand because the mana is spent on vampires. Deflecting Swat and Teferi's Protection sat uncast for a whole game (002), and the reason that matters is the structural one: a deck that cannot afford to hold up interaction is a deck that does not run interaction, whatever the list says.
Mulligan discipline. One mulligan, then kept a two-land hand out of stubbornness knowing at the time it should have gone back (002).

This pod runs heavy creature removal and heavy board wipes, and Ryan recurs artifact and enchantment removal — Anointed Procession resolved and was gone the following turn (002). It is still in the deck.
Tight lines get missed in the moment. I could have paid more life, faster, to pump the vampire and drawn a pile of extra cards off the death trigger (004).
Seat 5 in a five-player pod. My read is that the first-seat momentum advantage compounds with the mana deficit rather than just adding to it (002).

diagnosis.json says card draw is not what costs games. All three V1 games ended with vampires on board and nothing in hand (001, 002, 003), and 003 calls it 'not a new finding, it is the finding, again'. The twelve swaps were pointed at exactly that, and 004 is the only game since.
read.what_changed: V1 to V2 is the twelve-swap bloodline list, and 003 is where the direction was decided. After that game at Alex's the deck stopped being swarm typal and became lords and payoffs — a small number of bodies worth pumping, tokens demoted to the dig engine, white-black lifegain into lifedrain — and that note explicitly withdraws the token-conversion axis I had taken from 002. 004 is the one game on the current list. It did not end out of gas the way the three V1 games did (001, 002, 003): the bodies dying drew cards instead of just leaving the board, and the loss came from a tutored two-card infinite while Edgar was dominating (004). My own verdict on it was 'the refactor really showed'. One game, so read it as a first result, not a settled one. Two older details are superseded: 001's finisher turn ran through Olivia's Wrath and 003's opener set up Warleader's Call, and the swaps removed both, so those parts of those games no longer describe the deck I am holding.
